front: Which operator is central to implementing a Queue as a cyclic array (ring buffer)?
back: The modulo operator (%), to wrap the index back to 0 at the end of the array.

front: What's the amortized cost of push/pop on a dynamically-resizing array stack?
back: Θ(1) amortized — occasional O(n) resizes (doubling/halving) are spread out over many O(1) operations.

front: Name two real-world use cases each for stacks and queues.
back: Stacks: function call management, undo history, syntax parsing. Queues: task scheduling, buffering, breadth-first search.
A double-ended queue — allows insertion and removal at both ends.

front: Implementing a Queue with two Stacks (S1, S2): what does enqueue do, and what does dequeue do?
back: enqueue(x) always pushes onto S1 -- O(1). dequeue: if S2 is empty, drain all of S1 onto S2 first (reversing order), then pop from S2 -- O(n) worst case, but amortized O(1).

front: Implementing a Stack with two Queues: what invariant do the two queues maintain, and what does pop() do?
back: One queue is always empty. pop() dequeues every element EXCEPT the last from the non-empty queue into the other, then dequeues and returns that final element -- O(n).

front: Why is building a Stack from Queues (or vice versa) inherently expensive, in terms of FIFO vs LIFO?
back: Each ADT needs fast access to the element its counterpart actively buries: a Stack needs the LAST-added element (which a Queue hides behind everything in front of it), and a Queue needs the FIRST-added element (which a Stack buries under everything pushed since).
